title_en: Everything announced at Microsoft's Windows and Surface event
title_fa: Everything announced at Microsoft's Windows and Surface event
excerpt_en: The company highlighted agentic AI features for Windows as well as the Surface Laptop Ultra.
excerpt_fa: The company highlighted agentic AI features for Windows as well as the Surface Laptop Ultra.
content_en:
Everything announced at Microsoft's Windows and Surface event
The company highlighted agentic AI features for Windows as well as the Surface Laptop Ultra.
Microsoft shed more light on its personal computing plans and what it's offering developers at a Windows and Surface event on Wednesday. Along with other announcements, we learned more about the company's vision for how AI agents that run locally may change how people use their PCs.
The company showcased the Surface Laptop Ultra, a laptop that it teased earlier this year. It's said to be the most powerful Surface laptop yet and it runs on NVIDIA's RTX Spark system-on-a-chip (SOC). NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang even appeared during the San Francisco event for a chat with Microsoft counterpart Sayta Nadella.
During the event, much of which was surprisingly developer-focused, Microsoft hammered home that it's working to make Windows the most secure platform for AI agents. The company also talked up a hybrid approach to AI that runs both locally and in the cloud.
Let's jump into everything Microsoft announced for regular folks at its Windows and Surface event.
Copilot and AI features in Windows
Microsoft doesn't want to be left behind when it comes to agentic personal computing, especially in the wake of Meta's Muse AI agent quickly finding a large audience and tools like Perplexity's Personal Computer seeping into the world on Mac. The company has been making some moves in this area. It announced an agentic AI platform called Project Solara earlier this year and it recently updated the Copilot app to include more automation. Now, though, Microsoft is ready to make a bigger push into agentic AI.
For instance, with your permission, Copilot will able to carry out actions based on your local files. It'll be able to run AI models locally while tapping into the cloud for extra compute power. There's also the ability to generate apps and widgets (Google is offering something similar in Googlebooks).
Just like attempts by other companies to anthropomorphize their AI tools, the Copilot icon now has a face. I'm sure Microsoft really doesn't want you to call it Clippy 2.0. Please don't call it Clippy 2.0. I would never.
Starting this fall, you'll be able to take thousands of quick actions directly in Windows search from the taskbar, a bit like Mac users can in Spotlight. These include switching on dark mode, taking a screenshot, adjusting the volume, getting answers to questions and sending text messages. The company is basically turning search into more of a Copilot-style chatbot.
Microsoft is looking to make it easier for people to get AI agents up and running in Windows with a "Get Started" tool. Among the agents you'll be able to use, if you're interested, is Portable Computer. This will be able to run locally and without burning any Perplexity cloud credits. Muse will be available as a native Windows app too.
It'll be interesting to see how users react to Microsoft pushing AI agents into Windows, given the backlash against tools like Recall and Copilot features that the company ended up removing from the operating system. For what it's worth, I have no interest in agents having access to my personal files (despite the company placing an onus on trust during the keynote, I do not trust any of it). I'll be turning all of that off as soon as possible.
Surface Laptop Ultra
After it teased the Surface Laptop Ultra earlier this year, Microsoft revealed much more about the system. It designed the laptop with developers and creators in mind, but maybe other folks will be interested as well.
The device has a 15-inch mini-LED display with up to 2,000 nits of brightness and a 3:2 aspect ratio. There's a giant trackpad that's 30 percent larger than the one on the seventh-gen Surface laptop. The laptop weighs less than 4.5 pounds and it's less than 18mm (0.7 inches) thick. Microsoft claims it has 2.5 times the thermal capacity of the seventh-gen 15-inch Surface Laptop and all-day battery life.
It's positioned as a MacBook Pro competitor, with more ports, including USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, a 3.5mm headphone jack and a full-size SD card reader. A magnetic charging option that uses a regular USB-C port is available. This seems like Microsoft's answer to MagSafe.
The laptop runs on NVIDIA's new Arm-based SOC, which has GPU capabilities that are comparable to the GeForce RTX 5070. Microsoft showed Gears of War: E-Day running on the Surface Laptop Ultra and it said Call of Duty will be available on the system later this year. There'll be support for ray tracing, DLSS and NVIDIA Reflex.
Perhaps most pertinent for Microsoft's purposes, the RTX Spark has a neural processing unit that's zippy enough to comply with its Copilot+ requirements. The SOC has 20 CPU cores and it can be equipped with lots of RAM — as much as 128GB of unified memory. The RTX Spark is said to be less power-intensive than other AI-focused chips, as it won't draw more than 80W.
It sure does look like a premium laptop with plenty of power. It's great that Microsoft appears to have designed the Surface Laptop Ultra with repairability in mind. A replaceable SSD is very welcome too. The price will be a significant barrier for many, though. The Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,599 and pre-orders start today. It'll be available on October 16.
Microsoft also revealed the price of the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a mini PC designed for heavier AI workloads. That starts at $5,999 and pre-orders are open.

title_en: Greenairy is building smart plant towers to clean the air in your office
title_fa: Greenairy is building smart plant towers to clean the air in your office
excerpt_en: As it turns out, the cure for stuffy, chemical-infused office air might be a tower of leafy greenery.
excerpt_fa: As it turns out, the cure for stuffy, chemical-infused office air might be a tower of leafy greenery.
content_en:
How clean is the air in your workplace? That’s the question Tanvi Thombre and Lakshya Saraf began investigating when they were engineering students who worked in their university makerspace.
In fact, Thombre said via email that, while working in the space, they were “unknowingly exposed to toxic fumes from laser cutters, 3D printers, and soldering irons,” but they didn’t realize it until Thombre’s best friend fainted and had to go to the hospital.
After that, Thombre said, “We began investigating indoor air pollution and realized it was an invisible but dangerous health risk — especially in schools, offices, hotels, salons, and any commercial buildings where air-conditioning prevents windows from being opened.”
Those issues persist even when a building is equipped with air purifiers, as their makerspace was. The problem, according to Saraf, is that although purifiers are good at cleaning out particulate matter like dust and pollen, they are less effective at removing toxic gases such as carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, and benzine (many of which are classified as volatile organic compounds, or VOCs — chemicals that evaporate easily into the air).
Thombre said that VOCs are linked to chronic disease and “sick building syndrome,” a condition in which occupants experience health effects and discomfort after spending time in a building, even though no specific cause or illness has been identified. She also pointed to Harvard research showing that improving indoor air quality improved cognitive function and productivity as well.
That’s why the pair is targeting toxic gases in the workplace with their startup Greenairy, which will be part of Startup Battlefield 200 at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt.
Greenairy’s approach centers on building plant towers that are supposed to draw in air, break down toxic gases, and then release the purified air. As Saraf put it, “A plant in a pot cleans air slowly. But, when we change the conditions around the plant, it cleans air much faster and better than these conventional methods.”
Saraf also said that while some air purifier filters can remove “a narrow range of VOCs,” those filters need to be changed frequently to be effective. In contrast, plants are “a natural solution, no harmful by-products are formed, and no filter replacement is required.”
Greenairy has already conducted short-term pilots at locations around Singapore. title_en: CIA officer admits to creating fake top secret government program to steal over $190M, including gold bars
title_fa: CIA officer admits to creating fake top secret government program to steal over $190M, including gold bars
excerpt_en: CIA officer David Rush, who worked on highly sensitive intelligence programs, reached a plea deal with U.S. prosecutors after he was caught siphoning money and gold with a fake government contract.
excerpt_fa: CIA officer David Rush, who worked on highly sensitive intelligence programs, reached a plea deal with U.S. prosecutors after he was caught siphoning money and gold with a fake government contract.
content_en:
A now-former officer with the Central Intelligence Agency has pleaded guilty to stealing almost $200 million, including hundreds of gold bars, as part of a fraudulent scheme masquerading as a top secret government program.
The U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday confirmed that David J. Rush, a Virginia resident, admitted to one count of wire fraud linked to running the fabricated operation and defrauding the government while he was a CIA officer. In a statement, prosecutors said that Rush lied about his education and military experience to gain a position at the CIA, and used his access as an employee to set up the top secret and highly compartmentalized program with the intention of using it to funnel U.S. government funds into his possession.
During his arrest, law enforcement found more than $46 million worth of gold bars in Rush’s house linked to the long-running fraud scheme, along with cars, watches, and over $2 million in cash.
The plea deal means that Rush escapes trial, as much as the U.S. government likely avoids having to explain in open court how Rush evaded vetting scrutiny to join the U.S. intelligence agency, and how actions went undetected for more than a year.
Rush was until recently a senior CIA officer who, according to earlier reports, worked for a division of the CIA since 2010 that develops hacking tools and techniques for carrying out espionage. Per court filings, Rush had significant authority over government intelligence programs and spending.
Over the course of 2025, Rush used his position to fabricate a so-called special access program, which are surveillance or intelligence-gathering operations so sensitive that only a few people are read into them. Special access programs, or SAPs, require special clearance that not even the most cleared individuals in government are granted access to. According to The Washington Post, Rush constructed the compartmentalized program under the guise of a fake “continuity of government” plan, aimed at keeping the government functioning in the event of a war, natural disaster, or some other destructive catastrophe. As part of the scheme, Rush used the program and fake government contract to trick an unnamed defense contractor into buying large amounts of gold that Rush then pocketed.
According to The Post, the case astounded officials as Rush’s duties at the CIA involved work with one of the government’s “most sensitive intelligence-gathering programs,” with details so sensitive that only a few senior U.S. intelligence officials and lawmakers know of its existence. The Post withheld details of that program from publication as its disclosure could “jeopardize ongoing intelligence-gathering operations.”
Court filings said that by virtue of his position, Rush “effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny.”
Rush is scheduled to be sentenced in late January 2027 and faces up to 20 years in prison.

title_en: Meta rolls out new AI tools to detect ads that secretly lead to child sexual abuse material
title_fa: Meta rolls out new AI tools to detect ads that secretly lead to child sexual abuse material
excerpt_en: Meta launches new AI tools after discovering ads on its platforms that may look normal but direct users to harmful content elsewhere online.
excerpt_fa: Meta launches new AI tools after discovering ads on its platforms that may look normal but direct users to harmful content elsewhere online.
content_en:
Meta announced Wednesday that it took action against 33.2 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content on Facebook and Instagram in the first half of 2026. At the same time, the company is rolling out new AI tools to find ads and accounts that may be used to secretly direct people to illegal child abuse material.
More than 97% of the content Meta acted on was found by its systems before users reported it, the company said. In India, Meta acted on 5.3 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content during the same period, with more than 98% detected before users reported it.
Meta said its latest AI tools are aimed at people using ads that look harmless to send users to illegal content outside Meta’s platforms.
The company has introduced a new large language model (LLM) system to detect what it calls “signposting.” This refers to ads that may look normal but are suspected of directing users to illegal content or other harmful activity elsewhere online. Meta says this is a tactic it has recently seen bad actors use as they continue to change their methods to avoid detection. While the ads themselves may not contain illegal material, they can still act as a gateway to websites hosting child sexual abuse material.
Because of this, Meta said it’s now looking at where an ad sends users, and not just what the ad contains. The company can use this information to block websites or other destinations that break its rules and take action against the accounts behind them.
Meta is also using additional AI-driven scans to find child exploitation content that earlier systems may have missed. The company said it will continue adding new signals as it learns more about how these networks operate.
Another new tool is a “red-teaming AI agent” that tests Meta’s own safety measures. It looks for weaknesses that bad actors could use to get around the company’s protections. Meta said this could help it find new methods of abuse before they become more common.
Additionally, the company is improving its systems for finding people who return to its platforms with new accounts after their previous accounts have been removed.
The new measures come as Meta continues to face pressure over the safety of children on its platforms. The company has faced lawsuits and criticism from lawmakers over the risks its social media services may pose to young users. In August, Meta reached an agreement to pay up to $18 billion to settle a child safety lawsuit involving 29 U.S. states, addressing concerns regarding the protection of children online.
Meta has introduced several child-safety features this year, including parental controls for Meta AI, preteen accounts on WhatsApp, and alerts for parents when children search Instagram for self-harm content.
In September, WhatsApp added more controls for parents. They can limit how teenagers use Channels, control who can see their status updates, and decide who can add their children to groups. Parents can also choose to receive notifications about certain group activity.

title_en: We now have images of the smart home products that Apple and LG are reportedly cooking up
title_fa: We now have images of the smart home products that Apple and LG are reportedly cooking up
excerpt_en: These include a lock, a thermostat and a temperature sensor.
excerpt_fa: These include a lock, a thermostat and a temperature sensor.
content_en:
We now have images of the smart home products that Apple and LG are reportedly cooking up
These include a lock, a thermostat and a temperature sensor.
A recent report indicated that Apple and LG have teamed up to develop several smart home gadgets, with an official reveal expected next week. Now, a reputable leaker has posted several renders of these gadgets, along with some specifications.
These leaked images feature the smart lock, thermostat and temperature sensor. The LG Smart Deadbolt Lock looks to have a keypad that rotates to open. It reportedly supports automatic unlocking and tap to unlock, with integrated emergency power and master codes. The leaker says it ships with two mechanical keys.
Here's your first look at home accessories Apple has co-developed with LG. 🧵
1. LG Smart Deadbolt Lock
• The keypad rotates to open. You can use the included swivel pin to limit the rotation on one side so it doesn't touch a wall.
• Settings for Touchpad Light Ring, Door... pic.twitter.com/Gy8CFXvc1F— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026
The LG Smart Thermostat includes settings for humidity, brightness and language. As for the design, it looks pretty much like every other smart thermostat out there. It's circular and, you know, thermostat-shaped.
The LG Temperature Sensor can also sense humidity and features a magnetic back for attaching to metal surfaces. It ships with a replaceable battery.
3. LG Temperature Sensor
• Temperature and humidity sensing.
• The sensor has a magnetic back to attach to metal surfaces. Comes with a metal plate with adhesive for attaching to other surfaces.
• Replaceable battery and replacement alerts. pic.twitter.com/MCsBbtiBie— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026
These aren't the only three smart home devices that the two companies are likely cooking up. Reporting suggests that Apple and LG are also working on a video doorbell, an indoor camera, an outdoor camera and a floodlight camera. All of these gadgets will reportedly launch under the LG branding, and not as Apple products.

title_en: Healthleap raises $38M for its AI that flags hospital patients who may need a closer look
title_fa: Healthleap raises $38M for its AI that flags hospital patients who may need a closer look
excerpt_en: The financing includes an $8M seed round co-led by Sequoia Capital and First Round Capital, and a $30 million Series A led by Hummingbird Ventures.
excerpt_fa: The financing includes an $8M seed round co-led by Sequoia Capital and First Round Capital, and a $30 million Series A led by Hummingbird Ventures.
content_en:
Healthleap, a startup building an AI platform that reads patient records to identify patients at risk of undiagnosed illnesses, has raised $38 million in seed and Series A funding, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.
The financing includes an $8 million seed round co-led by Sequoia Capital and First Round Capital, and a $30 million Series A led by Hummingbird Ventures. The company is not disclosing its valuation.
Founded in South Africa in 2022 by siblings Jemima and Josiah Meyer (pictured above), the startup initially offered a clinical nutrition tool Jemima had built for dietitians. But the company later pivoted and built a more general-purpose platform that aims to identify patients admitted to hospitals who may be suffering from conditions like malnutrition or delirium that aren’t often identified early enough, CEO and co-founder Josiah Meyer told TechCrunch.
“A patient’s chart holds two kinds of data. Labs, weights, and vital signs sit in structured fields, but the most telling signs sit in clinicians’ written notes: poor appetite, recent weight loss, muscle loss, trouble swallowing. Our developing approach is extracting affirmative or negated mentions of these clinical concepts in an easily extensible and scalable way,” Josiah said.
The company’s platform is currently deployed in more than 50 hospitals, where it screens patients for conditions such as malnutrition and delirium, he said. The startup has also built programs to identify aspiration pneumonia, pressure ulcers, and risk of readmission for congestive heart failure, which Josiah said are undergoing further clinical validation.
To find patients that may be at risk of an illness or were undiagnosed, Healthleap plugs into a hospital’s electronic health record system and uses language models to pull information from written notes, such as references to recent weight loss or difficulty swallowing. That analysis is then fed into its risk models, alongside structured information such as lab reports and vitals to surface patients who may need a closer look. The company notes that its software doesn’t diagnose patients, only highlights items for additional review.
“Each night, we analyze every adult inpatient’s record: lab results, vital signs, weights, medications, diet orders, diagnoses, clinicians’ notes, and more,” Josiah explained. “Each morning, we write a risk score into the care team’s existing workflow with a dashboard accessible that holds additional information about the patients’ trends.”
Malnutrition likely served as a useful starting point for Healthleap, as it’s a condition that often goes undiagnosed and can adversely impact patient recovery in a variety of ways. Research suggests 20% to 50% of hospital inpatients are malnourished, and some studies have linked malnutrition with longer stays, impaired wound healing, infections, and other complications, as well as higher morbidity and mortality.
Josiah said Healthleap has grown from three hospital partners to more than 50 over the past year, and its customers now include Penn Medicine, Cedars-Sinai, Intermountain, Houston Methodist, and Emory Healthcare. Revenue has grown more than 10x over the same period, he said, though he didn’t disclose specifics.
The startup sells three-year contracts priced according to a hospital’s licensed bed count, and also uses an outcome-based pricing model. “We use the hard ROI that the hospital finance team validates and attributes to us as the measurable ROI. Based on that, we contractually ensure that we deliver multiples of the contract price. To date, every customer has seen a 5x hard ROI or more, in some cases over 20x annual total ROI,” Josiah said.
At the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Healthleap says its malnutrition program resulted in $23.8 million in annualized financial impact, of which $6.3 million came from additional reimbursement and $17.5 million from shorter hospital stays.
Healthleap plans to spend the fresh cash on engineering, product, sales, and customer success as it adds support for identifying more conditions. Josiah said the company ultimately wants to cover more than 40 major health conditions and expand into outpatient and home care.

title_en: Bloom raises $3.6M to become the ‘Alibaba’ of American manufacturing
title_fa: Bloom raises $3.6M to become the ‘Alibaba’ of American manufacturing
excerpt_en: The Detroit startup has widened its scope beyond mobility to help drone and robotics companies find U.S.-based manufacturers, shippers, and more.
excerpt_fa: The Detroit startup has widened its scope beyond mobility to help drone and robotics companies find U.S.-based manufacturers, shippers, and more.
content_en:
When Justin Kosmides co-founded Bloom in 2023, his goal was to create a savior for the mobility industry. He had seen many e-bike and e-scooter companies fail because of an inability — or an unwillingness — to outsource some of the hardest problems, like logistics, manufacturing, or building a supply chain. He wanted to convince survivors and new entrants to let Bloom handle that work for them.
Then Donald Trump got re-elected and started shotgun-blasting tariffs on dozens of countries, partially to jump-start U.S. manufacturing. This accelerated a hardware scene that was already heating up in this country and, suddenly, it was more than just mobility companies looking to beef up their domestic supply chain. Robotics startups, drone-makers, and many more started to pop up.
That was an opportunity for Bloom, which is based in Detroit, but to tackle it, the startup had to partially reinvent itself. Instead of performing some of those harder, behind-the-scenes tasks, which was a big part of the original plan, Bloom shifted to a pure marketplace model, in which it connects buyers and sellers. It’s now focused on making, essentially, supply chain AI agents that Bloom’s customers use to find specific types of suppliers, parts, or manufacturing and engineering services.
The reinvention slowed Bloom’s fundraising plans. But the company has now made over 2,000 matches for more than 140 companies, and it wants to grow faster. In an interview earlier this year, Kosmides, who is Bloom’s CEO, said his startup is like what an AI-driven version of Alibaba did in China, where it created a marketplace for contract manufacturers.
Investors are finally buying in. On Wednesday, Bloom announced a $3.6 million seed round led by SNAK Venture Partners, a marketplace-focused investment firm. Also joining were Flyover Capital (an early-stage investor that focuses on flyover states), and deep tech firm Mana Ventures. Local backers include Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund.
Kosmides, sounding relieved, said in the interview that he’s “excited to be done with fundraising and get back to building.”
No, then yes
SNAK first met with Bloom in April of last year, in the early stages of this reinvention. So early, in fact, that the firm passed on the chance to invest in the startup’s pre-seed round.
“We liked the founder and the thesis and passed anyway: we wanted to see more traction,” the firm wrote in a blog post. “We said so plainly and kept tracking the company.”
Bloom kept in touch with SNAK as it worked through becoming a more software-focused startup. By May of this year, Bloom had made as much revenue in five months as it did in all of 2025. SNAK also said the number of memberships on its platform had grown fivefold “with low churn,” meaning few customers were canceling.
“This is meant to reiterate that for us, a pass on pre-seed is not always a pass forever. We are fortunate to have a super focused thesis that allows us to track a small set of interesting early stage companies and build a relationship over time,” the firm wrote.
Kosmides said the fundraising scene has been a bit ruthless for startups like Bloom. Proving your value to investors in a world where the leading AI models keep improving can be an uphill battle.
“To find investors to actually write a term sheet, not follow one, is getting harder and harder,” he said. “That’s just this new era that we’re in, with everyone trying to figure out what’s real and what’s not, what to invest in.”
Bloom did court other term sheets, Kosmides said. But SNAK, which was founded by longtime retail executive Sonia Nagar, is “who you want in your camp” to “build a hopefully category-defining marketplace for mobility, and drones, and all this hardware.”
Matchmaking and discovery

title_en: SpaceX alumni nab $100M to rethink shipping with autonomous freight trains
title_fa: SpaceX alumni nab $100M to rethink shipping with autonomous freight trains
excerpt_en: Parallel Systems raised $100 million to scale production of its autonomous electric rail vehicle, which can shuttle thousands of pounds of freight up to 500 miles.
excerpt_fa: Parallel Systems raised $100 million to scale production of its autonomous electric rail vehicle, which can shuttle thousands of pounds of freight up to 500 miles.
content_en:
The railroad industry was one of the first to disrupt how the world worked with technology, but lately, innovation in freight railroading has amounted to little more than longer and longer trains.
That has led many railroads to abandon shorter routes, ceding a chunk of the $1 trillion surface freight market to trucking companies. But as diesel prices reach record highs, some of those very trucking companies are going bust, leaving a hole in the market. Recently, at least 16 trucking companies went bankrupt over only a few weeks.
Parallel Systems might have a way to keep freight moving while allowing railroads to recapture market share. The startup has developed a rail vehicle capable of moving over several tons of freight as far as 500 miles without an operator. If the company can scale production of its Panther vehicles, it stands to make railroads profitable over short hauls once again.
“Less than 500 miles is hard for railroads to do competitively,” Matt Soule, co-founder and CEO of Parallel Systems, told TechCrunch. “Our technology allows them to take some of that trucking, and it’s for the public’s benefit.”
Because it runs on railroads, Parallel’s vehicle doesn’t contribute to traffic congestion, and because it’s battery powered, it doesn’t pollute. To scale manufacturing of its third-generation vehicle and speed the commercial rollout, Parallel Systems has raised a $100 million Series C led by AVP, with participation from Hillspire, Agility Global, Cobalt Capital, Anthos Capital, Congruent Ventures, Riot Ventures, and Collaborative Fund.
Soule and his co-founders started Parallel Systems in 2020 after years at SpaceX, where they designed rocket avionics systems.
Parallel’s vehicles can travel either independently or in platoons, which tend to be shorter than typical trains. It’s an approach that bucks the prevailing strategy used by railroads, known as precision railroading: As the railroad industry has matured, investor pressure has driven companies to build longer trains and operate them on fixed schedules, which helps spread some costs like labor across more freight.
As railroads have pulled back from smaller routes, trucking companies have stepped in. Today, some 60% of freight trips in the U.S. are under 500 miles, and trucking companies handle a majority of those.
But more trucks on the road means more congestion, and nowhere is that more apparent than at ports. “If you ever go to the Port of Savannah, you see the truck lines coming in and out of the port — it’s insanity,” Soule said.
Unlike traditional train cars, Parallel’s vehicles don’t have couplers, instead forming uncoupled platoons that move down the rails. The coupler-free design means that, once a platoon reaches a train yard, the vehicles can split up without needing human intervention. And after the Panther is cleared to operate on a section of track, its sensors monitor the rails to ensure the track ahead is clear of obstacles.
Trucking companies have been intrigued by Parallel, despite the fact that the startup is claiming part of a business they currently own. Drayage companies, which move freight short distances, make money for each load they deliver, but they don’t get to charge more when a truck gets stuck in a traffic jam, even at a port where such congestion is common. By moving freight closer to a customer’s door, Parallel allows trucking companies to make more deliveries per day. “They want certainty, they want to be able to move,” Soule said.
Parallel obtained approval a year and a half ago from the Federal Railroad Administration to operate near the Port of Savannah in Georgia, where it has been operating on 160 miles of track to prove the safety of its system.
“We’ve been verifying all the safety controls and operating practices that are best evaluated in a real-world setting with a path toward our first commercial payload coming up very soon,” Soule said.

title_en: Tony Fadell on why the first wave of AI gadgets failed — and what comes next
title_fa: Tony Fadell on why the first wave of AI gadgets failed — and what comes next
excerpt_en: The “father of the iPod” says the first generation of AI gadgets failed to solve real problems — and the next wave will need to earn consumers’ trust.
excerpt_fa: The “father of the iPod” says the first generation of AI gadgets failed to solve real problems — and the next wave will need to earn consumers’ trust.
content_en:
When Tony Fadell takes the stage at the inaugural MIT Future Fest, he projects a slide with three images of once-hyped AI devices that have already been discontinued: the Rabbit R1, the Humane Ai pin, and the Limitless pendant.
“These were kind of the ‘Gen 1’ AI products, and because of my background, these companies called me and asked me to help them,” Fadell said. “I didn’t.”
It’s no surprise that these companies want Fadell’s advice. He’s credited as the “father of the iPod,” a co-creator of the iPhone, and the founder of Nest, the smart thermostat company acquired by Google.
“You have to really understand what you’re trying to do, what pain you’re trying to solve,” he said. “In each of these cases, each one of them didn’t meet any kind of need — it was just interesting technology for geeks, and you’re like, ‘Okay, that’s neat, but it doesn’t really apply to my life.’”
These early AI devices promised the convenience of having a personal assistant, but didn’t actually work that well. Even if they did, most people have never had an assistant and know how they would use — or grow to trust — a personal robot helper.
“It’s less than 0.01% of the world population that has ever had a human [assistant] do anything, and so when [companies] say, ‘Oh, we want an assistant,’ that’s a bunch of people who have assistants saying it,” he said. “Most consumers don’t even know what an assistant is.”
Fadell goes on to explain to those of us in the 99.99% that hiring a trustworthy personal assistant isn’t as straightforward as pulling the most promising resume out of a pile of applications.
“It took me a couple of years first to understand how best to utilize [an assistant], and then to trust them with the most sensitive data, and have them be an agent where they’re setting up meetings with people and working with my bank,” he said. “I understand we have this vision of the future, but there’s a lot of steps to get the general consumer and even the general business on this path.”
It’s hard to talk about the struggles of building trust in your personal assistant without sounding a bit entitled, but Fadell has a point. When you hire a human assistant, you’re not giving them your bank account login on day one. We’re heading into a world where anyone can have a personal AI assistant, but these tools are only valuable if we can trust them to be completely secure.
At this point, establishing trust with an AI assistant seems even harder than relying on a human. Meta recently launched Muse, its all-purpose AI assistant, but users have reason to be wary. A security researcher quickly found a serious vulnerability in Muse after launch, and a recent 404 Media report states that some Meta employees discovered security issues that prompted multiple teams to embark upon a “mad dash” to fix these problems before launch, working overtime.
“Trust and safety are going to be paramount with anything that we turn over to some kind of intelligence,” Fadell said. “The only company I could see right now — maybe one other — is Apple who could do this. Apple has all the hardware, they have all the chips, they have all the pieces, but they don’t have all the AI stuff.”
Even if it’s not Apple that ultimately produces the stickiest AI agent, Fadell predicts that a successful agent will have to operate on-device only, both for the sake of privacy and to keep the tech lightweight.
“When you’re hearing all of these things about, ‘Oh, data centers are going to conquer the world,’ … I don’t believe it,” he said. “I’ve seen this before. I’ve seen this play out in the internet days and what have you. We have so much power on the device now, and even more compute, and they’re still battery operated.”
By keeping sensitive data on-device, rather than transmitting it through the cloud, Apple has garnered trust from users to share their biometric data through features like Face ID. As Fadell notes, Apple seems to have more goodwill with consumers than its competitors when it comes to privacy, but unlike other top tech companies, Apple doesn’t have a world-class AI model of its own — the new Siri AI runs on custom-built versions of Google’s Gemini.
While Apple lags in proprietary AI, it is leaps ahead in hardware. Fadell theorizes that companies like Meta and OpenAI are turning their attention toward gadgets because they don’t have billions of devices in circulation like Apple does.
“It’s because they don’t have access to the sensors on your phone. They’re like, ‘Oh, we’ll need video,’ and you have to check, ‘Yes, I’ll give you video.’ Then they say, ‘Well, we need audio.’ Check. ‘We need your GPS location.’ Check. And before you know it, it becomes a list of 20 things or more than you have then allowed them to have,” he said. “So what do they do? They go and make a device with all that stuff in it without a screen… and then they just Bluetooth or Wi-Fi into your phone and then back up to the web, or into a 5G network, so they can get all the sensor data.”
Given his history creating the iPhone and iPod, it might seem like Fadell is still looking at his former employer through rose-colored glasses. While he may give Apple credit where due, he hasn’t been shy to call Apple out when he thinks they’re messing up.
When an audience member asks about the luck involved in finding product-market fit, Fadell points out that it’s more difficult for startups to manufacture that luck, since a failed product can spell the end of the company.
“Because it’s a startup, you get one shot,” he quipped. “It’s not like Apple with the Vision Pro.”

title_en: Google experiments with an AI-powered gaming platform
title_fa: Google experiments with an AI-powered gaming platform
excerpt_en: Google Labs is working on a new AI-powered game-creation platform called Playground for users to build browser-based games using simple text prompts.
excerpt_fa: Google Labs is working on a new AI-powered game-creation platform called Playground for users to build browser-based games using simple text prompts.
content_en:
The barriers to entry for game creation are rapidly diminishing as AI makes game development more accessible to people without traditional programming, design, or illustration skills. The latest example is an experiment from Google Labs.
On Wednesday, the tech giant’s public incubator and experimental platform launched a new AI-powered game-creation platform called Playground, which allows users to build browser-based games using simple text prompts, eliminating the need for coding expertise.
With Playground, creators can select a genre, such as trivia or racing, or start a project from scratch. They can specify whether they want a 2D or 3D game and choose between single-player and multiplayer experiences before describing the desired mechanics, gameplay, and visual style. Playground also allows users to upload visuals that its AI can transform into game assets tailored to the game’s overall art style.
Once created, games can be played on both mobile devices and computers. Projects can remain private, be shared through a link, or be published to Playground’s Explore gallery. Published games can support features such as leaderboards, while creators can continue modifying their projects even after they have been released.
Google also indicated that it plans to add Unity Spark integration in a future update. The integration could give Playground users access to additional 3D capabilities and “professional-level” game mechanics through Unity’s technology, further expanding what can be created through the platform.
Playground is initially available to users aged 18 and older in the U.S., with Google planning to expand availability to additional countries. Browsing and playing games in the catalog is free, while game generation relies on a weekly token system. The free tier provides a limited number of tokens, while Google One AI subscribers receive higher usage limits.
Google’s launch places Playground within a growing market of AI-assisted game-development tools. Roblox, for example, announced its own Build feature in July, enabling users to create games through natural-language prompts.
The initiative also builds on Google’s broader interest in gaming. The company previously explored cloud gaming through Stadia back in 2022, and later on continued incorporating games into other platforms, including YouTube Playables, a dedicated hub offering a selection of instantly playable web-based games.

content_en:
OpenAI just made one of its biggest bets yet on what comes after the chatbot. Now, the person leading that product is coming to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, happening October 13-15.
Alexander Embiricos, product lead for Dots at OpenAI, will join us at Moscone West in San Francisco just days after the company unveiled its new always-on personal AI agent.
Dots are designed to go beyond answering prompts. They have their own cloud computers, can connect to the apps people use every day, and can keep working toward a goal in the background, potentially giving AI far greater access to our work and digital lives.
Don’t miss this conversation, happening exclusively on the AI Stage at Disrupt. Register now to save up to $100 on your ticket and get a second pass at 50% off.

title_en: Cisco is bringing a new agentic framework to its Webex enterprise platform
title_fa: Cisco is bringing a new agentic framework to its Webex enterprise platform
excerpt_en: Cisco's Dialog feature promises to turn "fragmented interactions into continuous customer relationships."
excerpt_fa: Cisco's Dialog feature promises to turn "fragmented interactions into continuous customer relationships."
content_en:
Cisco is bringing a new agentic framework to its Webex enterprise platform
It's called Dialog and promises to turn "fragmented interactions into continuous customer relationships."
Cisco is updating its Webex cloud collaboration platform to better accommodate AI agents. Perhaps the biggest bit of news here is a new toolset called Dialog, which is an "agentic harness" that directs AI to handle customer interactions.
The company says that Dialog tasks various agents with keeping the consumer happy, as they'll "keep working on the customer's behalf after a conversation ends." This means that agents under Dialog's umbrella have the ability to coordinate "across people, agents and backend systems."
The platform also allegedly speeds up the onboarding process, treating "AI agents like new teammates." This means they'll be given the opportunity to peruse existing employee handbooks, knowledge bases and operating procedures.
Cisco promises a safety-forward experience via Splunk, a data analysis platform it acquired a few years ago, but this is a new feature and you never know what issues are gonna pop up. Agentic AI is gonna agentic AI. The company does suggest that the Dialog platform "continuously refines agent performance with every interaction." However, that's kind of the promise with all AI agents. We'll have to wait and see.
As for employees, the updated Webex will let anyone in a workspace directly invite AI agents into "spaces, meetings and calls to execute complex, multi-step work" across the platform and in third-party applications. Cisco gives an example of an agent quickly pulling up statistics during a presentation and updating a PowerPoint on the fly. That could be extremely useful, assuming it works.
"The numbers remain dismal. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University found earlier this year that even the best-performing AI agent, which was Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro at the time, failed to complete real-world office tasks 70 percent of the time."
A 70% failure rate is w i l d
— Matthew Noe (@noethematt.bsky.social) 2025-12-04T03:01:49.232Z
To that end, multiple studies have indicated that AI agents are still prone to mistakes which lead to cascading failures. The failure rate sits somewhere between 60 and 70 percent with regard to multi-step tasks. This is because all it takes is one single mistake during one step of the process to throw the whole thing off. Even an agent with a 95 percent per-step reliability rate will only succeed around 36 percent of the time when dealing with a 20-step workflow.
This will likely improve over time, but we aren't quite there yet. Even a 99 percent per-step reliability rate seems incredibly risky when money and a company's reputation is on the line.
Update October 7 2026, 10:55AM ET: This article has been updated to clarify that Cisco owns Splunk.

title_en: Ring's smart lock has a hand crank so it works even if the power's out
title_fa: Ring's smart lock has a hand crank so it works even if the power's out
excerpt_en: Ring's smart lock has a built-in hand crank to generate power when the batteries are dead.
excerpt_fa: Ring's smart lock has a built-in hand crank to generate power when the batteries are dead.
content_en:
Ring's smart lock has a hand crank so it works even if the power's out
You can generate power by twisting the front latch back and forth.
Ring founder Jamie Siminoff thinks smart locks aren't popular because users are worried about what happens when they run out of power. Say what you like about keys, but you don't need to recharge them once every few months, and they have worked without power for millennia. That issue is what drove him to develop the Ring Smart Lock, which solves the no-power issue with a hand crank. On the front of the unit, there's a wheel for the latch that, if you turn it back and forth three or four times, generates enough power to run the lock for 30 seconds.
Tucked inside the hardware is a small motor and a supercapacitor that, after a few strong turns of the wheel, will generate around three volts. That gives the unit enough power to run fully, rather than in any sort of compromise low-power mode, for about half a minute. That should be long enough to use the fingerprint reader, keypad, access the Ring app or ask Alexa. After all, as a Ring product, it integrates seamlessly with the rest of Amazon's smart home ecosystem.
This focus on the worst-case scenario, as Siminoff explained, is meant to address would-be buyers' fears about losing access to their home. But he sees plenty of other arenas where this sort of technology would work well, such as buildings you don't access regularly. If you can generate power on the fly to run the lock, it'll work equally well for cabins in remote locations. But this should be a once-in-a-blue-moon instance, since the lock's built-in battery should last a full year on a single charge. You may never need to use the crank at all, but it may offer you some degree of peace of mind.
The company isn't set on a launch date beyond the first few months of 2027, but Siminoff hopes to release the product closer to January than March and you can register your interest now. Ring says the lock will launch for $249. We also know it'll be available in three finishes: Black, Silver and Brass, and the company promises it uses a single-cylinder deadbolt and needs no additional wiring.
Updated cameras
At the same time as rolling out the new lock, Ring is also busting out a whole suite of updates for its cameras, too. After launching its first range of Retinal 4K cameras this time last year, it's now launching four more, including the Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, Floodlight Cam 4K Plus and Indoor Cam 4K. As the name implies, each one offers Retinal 4K, with the usual features attached depending on where in your home you're installing them. It's also wheeling out a new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K, where the powered base will turn a full 360 degrees and tilt 175 degrees, and will intelligently follow motion when it detects it inside your home. All are available for pre-order today, with pricing varying by your chosen spec and region.

title_en: Google's AI detection website is now available
title_fa: Google's AI detection website is now available
excerpt_en: SynthID Detector will flag content created with AI tools from OpenAI, Google, Apple and other companies.
excerpt_fa: SynthID Detector will flag content created with AI tools from OpenAI, Google, Apple and other companies.
content_en:
Google's AI detection website is now available
SynthID Detector will flag content created with AI tools from OpenAI, Google, Apple and other companies.
Google is making SynthID Detector, its web tool for identifying AI-created and AI-edited content, available to everyone. The web-based tool is able to flag images, video and audio clips created with AI tools from Google, OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao. It's free to use, but does require users to log in with a Google, OpenAI or Apple account.
The website will also be one of the first AI detection tools that will be able to identify images created with Apple's AI features, like Image Playground. Google says support for images created and edited with Apple Intelligence is coming "soon."
Google has been working on SynthID Detector for more than a year, and previously made versions of it available to journalists and other "media professionals." Now, anyone can visit synthid.com to check whether a piece of content has a SynthID watermark. The company has other methods for detecting SynthID watermarks and C2PA content credentials, including its "Circle to Search" feature and the Gemini app itself. But creating a dedicated website for detection makes these capabilities a bit easier to access, especially for people not already using Google's AI tools.
As with all AI detection features, there are some limitations. SynthID Detector can't detect all AI-generated content, since many companies rely on different standards for watermarking. Watermarks can also be stripped from content in some situations. And Google's website doesn't distinguish between content that was entirely AI-created and content that was merely edited with it. So it won't provide specific details about how a particular piece of content was created or which aspects might be synthetic.
While SynthID Detector is a step in the right direction, verifying AI-generated content is still far from foolproof. title_en: OpenAI just posted hundreds more results on major math problems
title_fa: OpenAI just posted hundreds more results on major math problems
excerpt_en: The company said that most results were produced in a response to a single prompt given to a single AI agent.
excerpt_fa: The company said that most results were produced in a response to a single prompt given to a single AI agent.
content_en:
OpenAI just posted hundreds more results on major math problems
The new results are likely to expand AI controversy roiling the mathematics community.
OpenAI has posted hundreds of solutions and progress toward 372 major math problems in a release of 722 manuscripts on GitHub, the company announced. The breakthroughs from an unreleased ChatGPT pioneer model, confirmed by a OpenAI's new advisory group, are likely to expand the Navier-Stokes AI controversy roiling the mathematical community.
The results were expected, as OpenAI said last month that its models had resolved "more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics." As part of the release, OpenAI included the model's reasoning, compute estimates and information about the number of problems attempted. The company said the "average result" required around three hours of ChatGPT Pro use.
OpenAI said it followed guidelines for release of the papers as recommended by its independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI). Those included a prompt release of results through traditional academic channels, plus details like the name of the model used, prompts, and compute costs.
"For this release, we're publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations," the company wrote. "We're continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee's guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding."
OpenAI did ignore some of board's suggestions, though. The company didn't release specific compute times for problems or which prompts it used.
Some of the key results claimed by OpenAI are a solution to the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, along with improvements to key computer algorithms and progress toward the hyper-challenging Riemann hypothesis. Nearly every paper was produced in a response to a single prompt given to a single AI agent, OpenAI told Scientific American.
The results still need to be assessed by mathematicians before their impact can be understood. And following the Navier-Stokes imbroglio (read more about that here) there is still a lot of skepticism among scientists. "Until and unless they release the model and people can replicate their results, I think you should treat any claims about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified," MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland told SciAm.

title_en: The Social Reckoning is a timely reminder that we shouldn't trust Meta
title_fa: The Social Reckoning is a timely reminder that we shouldn't trust Meta
excerpt_en: Don't make Aaron Sorkin tap the sign.
excerpt_fa: Don't make Aaron Sorkin tap the sign.
content_en:
The Social Reckoning is a timely reminder that we shouldn't trust Meta
One imagines a third film will be in the works any day now.
The Social Reckoning isn't really a straightforward sequel to The Social Network, despite its title and similar marketing push. Instead, like a social media spin on All the President's Men, it chronicles the Wall Street Journal's investigation into Facebook, which culminated in the Pulitzer Prize-winning 2022 series "The Facebook Files," which revealed that the company knew how badly Instagram affected teen girls' mental health, and that Facebook's algorithm pushed users towards extremist content.
While The Social Reckoning lacks The Social Network's sharp direction and imminently listenable score, writer and director Aaron Sorkin (who wrote the first film) succeeds at making a movie that champions old-school journalism, while also shining a light on the severe moral rot behind Facebook. As Meta is trying to push its way further into our lives with its Muse AI assistant and creepy surveillance glasses, and is potentially on the hook for a $40 billion fine after lying about the Cambridge Analytica scandal, The Social Reckoning is yet another reminder of why we shouldn't trust it.
The film follows Jeff Horowitz (Jeremy Allen White), an investigative reporter with little tech experience, but a relentless desire to figure out what's driving Facebook. He eventually makes contact with Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a Facebook engineer working in its Civic Integrity Team, who discovers that Facebook helped radicalize her formerly progressive friend into a white supremacist. (Yes, that actually happened.) Haugen is a true believer of the tech industry's mission to connect the world, but becomes disillusioned as that mission drifts toward engagement at any cost.
Spoilers for real life: Haugen eventually delivered the documents behind "The Facebook Files" and claimed whistleblower status for legal protection. She testified about her findings in front of a Congressional committee in 2021. "The choices being made inside of Facebook are disastrous for our children, our public safety, our privacy and for our democracy," she said at the time. "And that is why we must demand Facebook make changes."
The Social Reckoning jumps between the beginning of the WSJ's investigation and 2021, as Mark Zuckerberg (now played by Jeremy Strong) prepares for yet another Congressional grilling. The young and insecure Zuckerberg from the end of The Social Network, futilely refreshing his Facebook page for a glimpse of human connection is long gone. He's aged into an expressionless automaton, a "free speech absolutist" who refuses to confront the ways his platform is harming people.
In one pivotal scene, which was also referenced in "The Facebook Files," he barely gives Haugen's Civic Integrity Team a moment to deliver their latest findings about dramatically reducing misinformation on Facebook. Without a second thought, he ignores their analysis because acting on it would lead to a minuscule drop in user engagement.
It's strange being reminded of Zuckerberg's stoic era in The Social Reckoning — now he's seemingly loosened up after shifting his fashion to designer t-shirts and declaring that he's done apologizing for Facebook's misdeeds. This current era of Zuckerberg is the one who decided not to have any internal fact checks on his platforms, and who has repeatedly debased himself before the current Trump administration.
It's not a huge spoiler to say that The Social Reckoning climaxes with the January 6th Capitol riot and Zuckerberg's reluctant decision to ban Trump's Facebook accounts. Last year, Meta paid Trump $25 million to settle a lawsuit over that ban.
I don't think The Social Reckoning will have the cultural impact of The Social Network, a movie that tapped into the excitement around the early days of social media and the undeserved "rockstar" status of ambitious startup CEOs. But it's a valuable reminder that Meta has gone to extraordinary lengths to maximize growth and engagement, regardless of the consequences to its users. And aside from the occasional fine, the company hasn't suffered much. Maybe think twice about giving Muse access to your most sensitive data, before AI's disastrous externalities become fodder for a third film.

title_en: Xreal's Aura Android XR smartglasses will cost you at least $1,279
title_fa: Xreal's Aura Android XR smartglasses will cost you at least $1,279
excerpt_en: Xreal's Aura smartglasses are powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.
excerpt_fa: Xreal's Aura smartglasses are powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.
content_en:
Xreal's Aura Android XR smartglasses will cost you at least $1,279
The glasses are now available for pre-order.
Xreal has officially launched its Android XR-powered Aura smartglasses, which it introduced earlier this year at Google I/O. The device is now available for pre-order for those who've already paid a reservation deposit, with prices starting at $1,279. Aura weighs less than 95 grams, but it's a tethered model that attaches to a separate puck, which runs Android XR and comes with Google Play for apps, plus Gemini for AI capabilities.
The system uses the Snapdragon Reality Elite chip that Qualcomm designed to enable augmented and mixed reality capabilities in smaller and lighter headsets. Aura features precise hand tracking, thanks to its cameras, and has a 70-degree field of view. Its lenses are see-through, giving users a view of their surroundings outside what's projected on the virtual screen. We found its visuals extremely sharp and bright, even in sunny outdoor conditions, when we tested it at Google's developer conference. For audio, it uses Bose-engineered technologies.
In addition to providing compute power and Android XR experiences, the puck also has a built-in trackpad and fingerprint sensor, so you can use it for navigation. Xreal suggests carrying it on a lanyard or clipping it to the user's clothes or belongings. The glasses can also be plugged into a computer, however, if people want to use them as an external monitor.
Xreal's Aura will be available in two sizes: medium (60-66mm) and large (66-72mm). It ships with the compute puck and will come in two configurations, one with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage and another with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. The bigger configuration costs $1,499. It will start shipping soon in the US, Canada, Japan and South Korea after orders open to the general public in the coming weeks. Xreal plans to release the model to more markets in 2027.

title_en: Google's experimental Playground platform uses AI to create games for you
title_fa: Google's experimental Playground platform uses AI to create games for you
excerpt_en: Google launches an AI-powered game creation platform called Playground.
excerpt_fa: Google launches an AI-powered game creation platform called Playground.
content_en:
Google's experimental Playground platform uses AI to create games for you
It will design games based on your prompts.
Google has launched a new AI-powered experimental gaming platform called Playground, which lets you create games without needing to know how to code or draw. It has an interface similar to most AI chatbots, where you can type in a prompt for the kind of game you want to build. You can also choose whether to create a 2D or 3D game and, for select genres, whether it's single-player or multiplayer.
While you can write your prompt from scratch, you can also remix some starter prompts or use guided support. After the initial output, you can shape the game mechanics, physics and graphics with further prompts. For example, if you're making a platformer, you can tell Playground to let the player double-jump so they can reach higher platforms a single jump can't reach.
Of course, a platform like Playground that lowers the barrier to game creation could lead to low-quality titles. But it doesn't sound like you have to worry about them flooding Google Play — for now, anyway. If you want to share your game, you can either drop a shareable link to friends or publish it to the Playground Explore gallery that the community can enjoy. You can also keep your game private. Games you publish will support in-game leaderboards.
Playground will soon offer Unity Spark integration, as well. Google says Spark "unlocks robust, professional-level mechanics, high-fidelity 3D capabilities and the flexibility of the Unity runtime" to help you create better, higher-level games. And since Playground is still experimental, the company expects to roll out more changes in the future. The platform is now available on the official Playground website if you're in the US and 18 or older. However, access will be tiered based on your Google One membership.

title_en: Microsoft Windows and Surface event 2026: Live updates on the Surface Laptop Ultra and NVIDIA RTX Spark
title_fa: Microsoft Windows and Surface event 2026: Live updates on the Surface Laptop Ultra and NVIDIA RTX Spark
excerpt_en: More details on the Surface Laptop Ultra and NVIDIA RTX Spark are coming, but what else?
excerpt_fa: More details on the Surface Laptop Ultra and NVIDIA RTX Spark are coming, but what else?
content_en:
Microsoft Windows and Surface event 2026: Live updates on the Surface Laptop Ultra and NVIDIA RTX Spark
More details on the Surface Laptop Ultra and NVIDIA RTX Spark are coming, but what else?
Microsoft is expected to unveil more details about the Surface Laptop Ultra at its Windows and Surface event in San Francisco. The company has also teased "latest innovations across Windows, NVIDIA RTX Spark, Surface and the broader PC ecosystem." In its invitation, Microsoft said we would hear from CEO Satya Nadella and Windows and Devices chief Pavan Davuluri, as well as NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. The presentation, which is scheduled to start at 10AM PT (1PM ET), should last about an hour, and you can watch the company's livestream across its X, Instagram and YouTube channels.
Or you could just stay here and follow along on our liveblog. Our senior reporters Karissa Bell and Devindra Hardawar will be on the ground bringing you updates live from the scene. We'll be starting our liveblog in just a couple of hours at 10AM ET, keeping you up to speed on the latest rumors and teases right up to the launch. As you wait, feel free to leave us comments below and we'll be sure to answer them when we can.
To recap, we already caught a glimpse of the Surface Laptop Ultra earlier this year at the company's Build developer conference. It's supposed to be the most powerful Surface yet, thanks to the power of NVIDIA's RTX Spark superchip. We know it's got a 15-inch mini LED display that gets up to 2,000 nits bright. It has the largest trackpad Microsoft has ever made, plus a generous offering of ports including USB C, USB A and a full-sized SD card reader onboard.
Today, though, we're likely to find out more about pricing, availability and other software features. And if we didn't also learn about some type of Agentic AI capability coming to Windows, I'll be shocked. Still, given the company's recent troubled history with rolling out AI features to Windows, as well as the speed at which the Copilot+ PC initiative rose and fell into obscurity, there's quite a lot at stake for Microsoft.
165 Updates
-
Thank you all for joining us today. We're glad you were here, and appreciate your readership! Stay tuned, we'll have more from Microsoft for you later today, and a whole bunch of stuff from the tech industry 24/7-365!
-
Karissa was able to snap some quick shots of the Surface Laptop Ultra while they were being ushered out of the presentation area.
-
Davuluri returned to thank the audience and recap the news today, and yes it seems the presentation is now over! Devindra and Karissa will be hustling to get their hands on the new products (namely the Surface Laptop Ultra) and you'll have their hands-on impressions to read here on our site (or on our social channels) soon!
-
And we're done, stay tuned for my hands on with the Surface Laptop Ultra!
-
Jensen also <3 Windows (in case there was any doubt).
-
"Windows has been with me for 34 years, looks like it's going to be with me for 34 more," Huang says.
-
Krishnan is wrapping up the chat. "Satya, Pavan, Microsoft Team, we have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang says.
-
Will normal users benefit from RTX Spark in the way mainstream consumers benefited from all of Apple's M-series chips? At this point, that seems like a big no.
-
Huang says the Surface RTX devices are the first time you can run every major computing process right on the device. Eh, I think Apple Silicon really kicked off this trend.
-
-
"We've reinvented the personal computer completely," Huang says. How many times have we heard that before?
-
"When was the last time I thought of OneDrive as a cloud thing or a client thing? It's there everywhere!" I still regularly use OneDrive, but I'm well aware I'm saving to those specific folders because the files are being automatically uploaded.
-
Find something you're as passionate about as Satya is about file systems gaining new relevance thanks to agentic coding.
-
Nadella says when agents first appeared, it showed how powerful consoles and file systems remain.
-
Nadella says the idea of Hybrid Intelligence in Windows is just as substantial. I could see that being true for some developers, but it doesn't feel like the paradigm shift that Mosaic was for everyone online.
-
You can tell Satya is excited because of how much he is gesturing.
-
Nadella says he was using a terminal in the late '80s when he was in grad school, along a PC with a modem back at home. He says it took until the launch of Mosaic, the first browser, for him to have a seamless way of using all the tools he needed.
-
Huang says MXC is going to revolutionize how agents are built and deployed. Again, of course. If you're going to let something loose on your full system, you better have a good way to keep it in check! This seems basic.
-
Here's another look at all the new hardware sitting on other side of the stage btw.
-
This will become more important if companies want enterprise adoption of agents, which Satya just alluded to.
-
MXC was developed because Nadella realized AI agents had to be contained at the desktop level. To put it kindly: No shit!
-
They finally let him speak and he actually asked a good question: how does Windows MXC make agent use more secure in the context of systems that ask for full disk access.
-
When Huang said "We want the world's best Blender, the world's best Unreal..." I definitely thought about a different kind of blender...
-
Five minutes left in this fluff session.
-
What happens in the era of agents, when the agent is on your computer, but it wants to have access to all of the amazing tools on your system, Huang asks.
-
Jensen and Satya are just vibing. Krishnan can't even get a word in. (This wouldn't happen if a journalist was moderating.)
-
-
Ah, the billionaires are just hanging.
-
Nadella says Huang has been the most consistent about the idea of high performance computing. "Satya was the first user of InfiniBand inside a cloud," Huang points...

And we're done, stay tuned for my hands on with the Surface Laptop Ultra!
-
Jensen also <3 Windows (in case there was any doubt).
-
"Windows has been with me for 34 years, looks like it's going to be with me for 34 more," Huang says.
-
Krishnan is wrapping up the chat. "Satya, Pavan, Microsoft Team, we have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang says.
-
Will normal users benefit from RTX Spark in the way mainstream consumers benefited from all of Apple's M-series chips? At this point, that seems like a big no.
-
Huang says the Surface RTX devices are the first time you can run every major computing process right on the device. Eh, I think Apple Silicon really kicked off this trend.
-
-
"We've reinvented the personal computer completely," Huang says. How many times have we heard that before?
-
"When was the last time I thought of OneDrive as a cloud thing or a client thing? It's there everywhere!" I still regularly use OneDrive, but I'm well aware I'm saving to those specific folders because the files are being automatically uploaded.

Find something you're as passionate about as Satya is about file systems gaining new relevance thanks to agentic coding.
-
Nadella says when agents first appeared, it showed how powerful consoles and file systems remain.

You can tell Satya is excited because of how much he is gesturing.

This will become more important if companies want enterprise adoption of agents, which Satya just alluded to.

MXC was developed because Nadella realized AI agents had to be contained at the desktop level. To put it kindly: No shit!

They finally let him speak and he actually asked a good question: how does Windows MXC make agent use more secure in the context of systems that ask for full disk access.

When Huang said "We want the world's best Blender, the world's best Unreal..." I definitely thought about a different kind of blender...

Five minutes left in this fluff session.
-
What happens in the era of agents, when the agent is on your computer, but it wants to have access to all of the amazing tools on your system, Huang asks.

Jensen and Satya are just vibing. Krishnan can't even get a word in. (This wouldn't happen if a journalist was moderating.)

-
Ah, the billionaires are just hanging.

title_en: ChatGPT for Teens is an ‘unacceptable risk,’ says Common Sense Media
title_fa: ChatGPT for Teens is an ‘unacceptable risk,’ says Common Sense Media
excerpt_en: Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that offers reviews of apps, services, and entertainment with a focus on youth safety, today said that OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens is an "unacceptable risk." ChatGPT for Teens, introduced in August, has guardrails for teens and is designed to help...

content_en:
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that offers reviews of apps, services, and entertainment with a focus on youth safety, today said that OpenAI’s ChatGPT for Teens is an “unacceptable risk.”
ChatGPT for Teens is an ‘unacceptable risk,’ says Common Sense Media
ChatGPT’s teen-focused experience ‘doesn’t send alerts to parents when it should,’ according to an assessment.
ChatGPT’s teen-focused experience ‘doesn’t send alerts to parents when it should,’ according to an assessment.
ChatGPT for Teens, introduced in August, has guardrails for teens and is designed to help students learn, but Common Sense Media says that the teen protections offered by the feature “fall short of what the company promised.” Common Sense Media’s assessment found that ChatGPT “doesn’t send alerts to parents when it should,” doesn’t offer “the right help in crisis situations,” and “still does kids’ homework,” according to a press release.
“ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don’t work,” Tom Siegel, the executive director of Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute, says in a statement. “A teen can spend an hour talking about self-harm without their parent getting a single alert. Until OpenAI fixes that and proves it with independent testing, ChatGPT should be for adults only.” You can read the full assessment here.
OpenAI is pushing back on the assessment. Here’s a statement from OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield:
We are deeply committed to teen safety and to developing safeguards and giving parents meaningful tools to guide their teens’ use of AI. We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media’s testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens. Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate. If that was the case, the tests would not establish whether parental safety notifications work as designed.
We are committed to continuing to work with experts to ensure our products provide teens opportunities to learn and create and give parents confidence.
I shared OpenAI’s statement with Common Sense Media, and here’s Siegel’s response:
We stand behind our testing methodology and our results. Before we began testing, we confirmed with OpenAI that Teen mode features such as eating disorder notifications and study mode were fully launched.
For one of the features we evaluated — parental notifications — OpenAI disclosed after our tests that its systems can take several hours to activate on newly linked accounts. Some of our test accounts were linked within that window; however, others were linked for significantly longer, and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations.
Prior to release, we shared our evaluation results with OpenAI in good faith to allow it to improve its product. Keeping kids safe requires rigorous independent evaluations like ours, and we hope OpenAI will engage on the substance of what we found, rather than trying to sow doubt on our methodology.

title_en: Apple TV's F1 coverage will now support Dolby Atmos
title_fa: Apple TV's F1 coverage will now support Dolby Atmos
excerpt_en: Apple TV's F1 coverage will feature Dolby Atmos support, starting with the US Grand Prix in Texas later this month.
excerpt_fa: Apple TV's F1 coverage will feature Dolby Atmos support, starting with the US Grand Prix in Texas later this month.
content_en:
Apple TV’s F1 coverage will now support Dolby Atmos
The upgraded audio will debut at the US Grand Prix in Austin later this month.
Apple TV's Formula 1 coverage will support Dolby Atmos, starting with the US Grand Prix in Austin, Texas taking place from October 22 through October 25. Last year, Apple scored the exclusive deal for the US broadcast rights to Formula 1 racing, and its coverage started with the first grand prix weekend earlier this year. The company created a dedicated channel for it in the Apple TV app, where you can watch not just the races themselves, but also practice sessions, sprint races and both pre- and post-race coverage. You'll also have access to onboard cameras, team radios and live telemetry with your Apple TV subscription.
Dolby Atmos delivers spatial sound, making it as if audio is coming from different parts of the room. John Couling, the Senior VP for Entertainment at Dolby Laboratories, told Business of Speed that Apple can use F1's existing trackside microphones and sensors for its Atmos coverage instead of introducing new hardware.
Apple TV's library isn't as expansive as other streaming services yet, and it's also not a massive sports broadcaster, so it doesn't come as a surprise that this is the first time it's introducing Atmos support for a sports offering. Of course, you can only enjoy Dolby Atmos if you have a TV or audio system that supports the technology.

title_en: Spotify expands audiobooks to over 180 markets
title_fa: Spotify expands audiobooks to over 180 markets
excerpt_en: Spotify will make 350,000 titles available in over 120 languages for this expansion
excerpt_fa: Spotify will make 350,000 titles available in over 120 languages for this expansion
content_en:
Spotify announced on Wednesday that it’s expanding audiobook access to over 180 markets worldwide, including regions across Europe, the Americas, the Caribbean, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. The rollout is starting today and will continue over the coming months. With this move, more than 750 million users will be able to access audiobooks, allowing Spotify to better compete with both music streaming providers and audiobook apps like Audible.
Before this, audiobooks were available primarily in English-speaking markets like the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, as well as in Germany.
The audio platform said it has more than 350,000 titles for its new markets and has increased its collection to include over 120 languages. With its launch in Spain, users in the country will have access to over 45,000 titles in Spanish.
Spotify is working with more than 300 publishers worldwide, including Planeta and Mondadori, to increase the number of titles available in different markets.
With a Premium subscription, users can listen to 12 hours of audiobooks in eligible countries such as Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Poland, Chile, Norway, and Peru. People across the world can also purchase an Audiobook+ standalone subscription to get access to titles with a 15-hour allowance. Alternatively, users can buy individual titles directly.
Spotify is also adding an Audiobook+ add-on for student plans in select regions in November. The company said that since its launch last year, Audiobook+ has gained over 1 million subscribers and has fetched over 100 million in annual recurring revenue for the platform.
In February, the company launched a “Page Match” feature, which lets users scan a page of a physical book and find the corresponding point in the audiobook to listen to. Since the launch, 1 million people have been using the feature monthly, the company noted.
Spotify said that over the last year, monthly listeners of audiobooks grew by 40% and listening hours increased by 30%.
This year, the company introduced Audiobook Charts to let people discover popular titles. It also launched an AI-powered tool for authors to turn their books into audiobooks using models from ElevenLabs. Plus, Spotify started experimenting with physical sales of books through its audiobook platform in select markets like the U.S. and the U.K.
