title_en: Why don't you see external antennas on mesh Wi-Fi systems?
title_fa: Why don't you see external antennas on mesh Wi-Fi systems?
excerpt_en: Mesh systems tend to look more like minimalist decor than traditional routers, and there's actually a good reason.
excerpt_fa: Mesh systems tend to look more like minimalist decor than traditional routers, and there's actually a good reason.
content_en:
Why don't you see external antennas on mesh Wi-Fi systems?
Mesh systems tend to look like minimalist decor.
In just about any space larger than an apartment, it's hard to deny the value of mesh Wi-Fi routers. They do have drawbacks — primarily their price-to-performance ratio — yet top speed is meaningless if coverage isn't consistent. You might liken it to owning a Porsche 911 in a place like the West Texas desert, where gas stations are so far apart that you could conceivably run dry on a high-speed drive.
Something we hadn't really thought about much until recently is the fact that most mesh routers are missing external antennas. They do have antennas, naturally — they're just under the surface. You'd think, though, that with coverage being a priority, gear makers would want every possible boost to signal strength.
As it turns out, burying antennas is not only fine, but actually a technical advantage given the goals of mesh systems. There are also additional business factors, although this is one case in which companies aren't cutting corners. You're likely getting a better product.
The benefits of your mesh router's internal antennas
Although external antennas do maximize range, that's actually less of a priority with mesh systems, for a reason that's glaringly obvious when you think about it for a second: A mesh network is already designed to repeat signals and fill in gaps. The most distant devices a mesh router has to talk to are usually its siblings, establishing a backhaul connection to your main router. All other devices are going to be a room or two away, at most.
Where things get interesting is the nature of internal antennas. These are often omnidirectional rather than focused, which aids in another important element of mesh technology: seamless connection and handover. With a wide net, routers can quickly detect nearby devices and switch connection duties, maintaining relatively consistent bandwidth the entire time.
In fact, there's higher potential for things to go wrong with external antennas. If they're adjustable, misaligning them can reduce connection strength to some devices. And let's not forget that external antennas are long and can be broken, whether that's during a move or by accidentally knocking a router off a tall surface. If you don't need to introduce these risks, it's logical not to.
Speaking of fragility, it's worth noting that better mesh routers may actually need more antennas than usual, since they provide a dedicated backhaul instead of splitting that bandwidth with your devices, slowing them down. A forest of external antennas would become not just more vulnerable, but unsightly and complex to manufacture. More on these points in a moment.
There are downsides to internal antennas. Apart from sacrificing range, there is hypothetically more potential for interference from nearby components. As you can tell, however, this issue has been dealt with in a way that minimizes any impact.
Boiling it down to the cool factor
Manufacturing costs offer an incentive to move things inside, too. External antennas naturally require more parts and materials. For an individual router, the price increase is going to be negligible. But spread across thousands or even millions of units, the bill quickly adds up. Considering the networking advantages, moving antennas inside is a win-win scenario for mesh Wi-Fi vendors.
Even better, internal antennas permit minimalist designs that a lot of shoppers find appealing. That's particularly important when you're going to have two or three units scattered through your home. For optimal performance, any router also needs to sit out in plain sight, and it might be easier to sell your partner on that with something that looks decorative, rather than like the radio tower it actually is.

title_en: Apple iPhone Duo vs. Motorola Razr Ultra: How do these foldables compare?
title_fa: Apple iPhone Duo vs. Motorola Razr Ultra: How do these foldables compare?
excerpt_en: The market seems to be overflowing with foldable phones, and the iPhone Duo and Moto Razr Ultra are top competitors.
excerpt_fa: The market seems to be overflowing with foldable phones, and the iPhone Duo and Moto Razr Ultra are top competitors.
content_en:
Apple iPhone Duo vs. Motorola Razr Ultra: How do these foldables compare?
Not all foldables are created equal.
It's no secret that Apple is late to the foldable phone party, but that's really its style, contrary to some myths. While it helped pioneer categories with the iPod, iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, more often than not Apple tends to sit on the sidelines, waiting for rivals like Samsung to take the big risks with new technologies. Then it swoops in, hopefully with a more polished product. The iPhone Duo is a prime example.
The foldable market is old enough at this point that Motorola has produced several generations of updated Razrs, its flagship being the 2026 Razr Ultra. At $500 less than the $2,000 iPhone Duo, there's obvious appeal, all the more so because you're not locked into the Apple ecosystem. Some of us are certainly OK with that predicament. In the Android world, though, you're not counting on one brand to get its hardware right every year.
If you're neutral on your platform pick for a future foldable, you should at least briefly pit the Ultra and Duo against each other. Given some dramatic differences, however, you're liable to end up firmly on one side of the fence. The two products are targeting very different demographics.
A battle of... passports and candybars?
The deepest split is in form factors. While both devices offer internal and external screens, with adaptable interfaces based on how they're folded, the Ultra assumes a standard candybar layout when open, measuring 7 inches diagonally. The goal is to provide a maximally compact device that's easier to slip into your pocket or a handbag, even if it means sacrificing some functions on its external screen. The Duo, meanwhile, is shaped like a passport. It operates like a regular iPhone when closed, and it opens up to provide a matte, iPad-like 7.6-inch display. It can't literally run iPad apps, but this nevertheless expands the functionality of compatible iPhone software, in some cases enabling split-screen multitasking. If you're expecting to get more work done with a foldable, the Duo wins by default.
Performance
Performance-wise, the devices are closer than you might think. We haven't benchmarked the Duo yet, since it's not shipping until October 23, but the Ultra comes equipped with a fast Snapdragon 8 Elite processor and 16GB of RAM. The Duo will likely rank faster thanks to Apple's newer A20 Pro chip and usual iOS optimizations. For the vast majority of apps, however, there shouldn't be a huge difference.
Cameras
The devices are superficially comparable in terms of cameras, with each having two rear shooters — one wide, one ultra-wide — Apple's being rated at 48 megapixels, and Motorola's at 50. The devil is in the engineering, though. iPhone cameras are typically some of the highest-rated in the industry, so we won't be surprised if the Duo continues that trend and trounces the Ultra, which has known issues versus competitors like Google's Pixel series.
On the other hand, the Ultra's front camera also slots in at 50 megapixels, whereas the Duo's is capped at 12. The Duo does have an additional under-screen internal camera, yet that may actually be worse. Apple isn't even sharing its megapixel count and is selling it primarily as a tool for FaceTime video calls. Selfie addicts are going to want to unfold and flip the Duo to use those rear sensors.
Battery and durability
The Ultra's battery lasted 31 hours in our video-based testing, and Apple claims a comparable amount for the Duo when using the internal display. Both phones should last a full day in mixed usage, in other words. Regarding toughness, both use hardened ceramic glass to protect the exposed front display; however, the Duo has a superior IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, versus the Ultra's IP48. To translate, they can both be submerged in fresh water for a short time — it's just that the Ultra is potentially vulnerable to dust particles under a millimeter. You'll probably be fine if you don't take your phone into the Sahara.
Pick your platform poison
Spec-wise, the two devices are close enough that your decision will probably boil down to three factors: price, software and use case. The Ultra's $1,500 is already too much for a lot of smartphone shoppers, never mind $2,000. You can actually spend up to $3,200 if you want to max out the Duo's storage. In theory, the Duo can replace both an iPhone and an iPad mini, so its sticker shock might have a little less sting.
If you inherently prefer iOS or Android, there's no compelling reason to switch here. The iPhone 18 Pro is available if you want a cheaper (non-folding) candybar phone, and Android fans are spoiled for book-style foldables, such as Motorola's own Razr Fold. It's probably wiser to look at that one first, particularly since $1,900 is still cheaper than $2,000. Let's not forget the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, either. The latter shares the same passport design as the Duo.
It may be worth taking a step back and questioning your reasons for getting a foldable. If you've got so little bag or pocket space that the Ultra is appealing, it might be wiser (and cheaper) to rethink your clothing and accessories. If you genuinely care about productivity, you can probably get more done by pairing an iPhone 18 Pro with a MacBook Neo, and actually save a little cash versus a Duo.

To translate, they can both be submerged in fresh water for a short time — it's just that the Ultra is potentially vulnerable to dust particles under a millimeter. You'll probably be fine if you don't take your phone into the Sahara.
Pick your platform poison
Spec-wise, the two devices are close enough that your decision will probably boil down to three factors: price, software and use case. The Ultra's $1,500 is already too much for a lot of smartphone shoppers, never mind $2,000. You can actually spend up to $3,200 if you want to max out the Duo's storage. In theory, the Duo can replace both an iPhone and an iPad mini, so its sticker shock might have a little less sting.
If you inherently prefer iOS or Android, there's no compelling reason to switch here. The iPhone 18 Pro is available if you want a cheaper (non-folding) candybar phone, and Android fans are spoiled for book-style foldables, such as Motorola's own Razr Fold. It's probably wiser to look at that one first, particularly since $1,900 is still cheaper than $2,000. Let's not forget the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, either. The latter shares the same passport design as the Duo.
It may be worth taking a step back and questioning your reasons for getting a foldable. If you've got so little bag or pocket space that the Ultra is appealing, it might be wiser (and cheaper) to rethink your clothing and accessories. If you genuinely care about productivity, you can probably get more done by pairing an iPhone 18 Pro with a MacBook Neo, and actually save a little cash versus a Duo.

title_en: Bluesky wants to give you your own domain on the open web
title_fa: Bluesky wants to give you your own domain on the open web
excerpt_en: Bluesky says the process will still take 18-24 months, so don't expect your new, shortened 'bsky' handle any time soon.
excerpt_fa: Bluesky says the process will still take 18-24 months, so don't expect your new, shortened 'bsky' handle any time soon.
content_en:
Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider teased long-term plans on Monday when he shared that the company has applied to make “.bsky” an internet domain suffix, like .com or .org. If approved, users will be able to turn their longer social handles into shorter, cleaner domain names.
For instance, instead of @sarahp.bsky.social, my handle could one day become just “sarahp.bsky.”
That could leave Bluesky room to innovate around user profiles, turning them from a simple page that houses someone’s bio and their posts into a more comprehensive personal home page that establishes someone’s online presence.
Bluesky’s application hasn’t been approved yet. Schneider said that ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers), the nonprofit that oversees domain names for the internet, will publish the applications for the new domains on October 7, 2026, and Bluesky’s request will be among them. It’ll take 18 to 24 months for the process to be completed.
Reached for comment, Bluesky said it hasn’t finalized how .bsky domains would be requested, registered, or distributed, but the company did say it had no plans to either sell or monetize the domains.
That’s a notable decision given that domain registration can be a profitable business that could serve as a potential revenue stream for a startup that has raised significant funds but isn’t (yet?) generating ad revenue.
However, Bluesky says selling domains goes against its belief in an open web.
“Domains are a big part of the open web, as they allow users to control their own online identity,” said Rose Wang, Bluesky’s COO, in a comment shared with TechCrunch. “Bluesky was built on the belief that you should own your presence online, not rent it from a platform that can take it away.”

title_en: Emmys will move from broadcast TV to Prime Video in 2027
title_fa: Emmys will move from broadcast TV to Prime Video in 2027
excerpt_en: Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will be able to watch the awards show on the platform.
excerpt_fa: Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will be able to watch the awards show on the platform.
content_en:
Amazon announced on Tuesday that Prime Video will be the new home for the Emmy Awards, marking another major Hollywood awards show’s move from broadcast television to streaming. This will also be the first time that the ceremony has had a dedicated home, as the show rotated across broadcasters like ABC, CBS, Fox, and NBC over the past seven decades.
Prime Video will stream the awards show worldwide for six years for free, starting in 2027, where it will go live in over 240 countries and territories. Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will also be able to watch the awards show on the Prime Video platform.
The terms of the deal were not disclosed.
The move comes as the Emmys face potential viewership declines, as more of its audience moves to streaming services. This year’s ratings for the 78th primetime Emmy Awards on NBC were down nearly 10% from the year prior, after a couple of years of growth, the AP reported. However, the telecast’s 6.87 million viewers this year were higher than its all-time low of 4.3 million in January 2024.
The Emmys aren’t the only major awards show making the shift to streaming. Last year, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal giving YouTube the rights to stream the Oscars beginning in 2029, while Netflix has streamed the Screen Actors Guild Awards since 2024.

title_en: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals
title_fa: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals
excerpt_en: French AI lab Mistral AI has released Mistral Large 4, a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals.
excerpt_fa: French AI lab Mistral AI has released Mistral Large 4, a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals.
content_en:
The race between open and closed AI is on, and Europe is still in the mix. On Tuesday, French AI lab Mistral AI released Mistral Large 4 (ML4), a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals — following what French president Macron described as “a third way in AI.”
Amid a growing divide between closed models that can be unplugged and open models that are often made in China, Mistral is positioning ML4 as an alternative to both. Nicknamed Le Chonk in reference to its 1 trillion parameters, ML4 is definitely not small; but is not an open-weight model yet. For the time being, it can only be accessed via a public guardrail endpoint, but Mistral plans to make its weights available in just three weeks, after safety testing is complete.
“In the meantime, we’ll work with trusted partners and governments to make sure that the open source weights can be used to defend, but not to [perform] malicious attacks,” Mistral VP Science Pierre Stock told TechCrunch.
Security concerns have been mounting in recent months, particularly among Mistral’s core audience — enterprises and institutions. At the same time, an open-weight model is easier to audit, Stock said.
Another important behind-the-scenes aspect is that ML4 was trained entirely on Mistral’s compute; using only 4,000 Nvidia GPUs “which is two to three times less than our Chinese competitors, and significantly less than the closed source competitors,” Stock said.
With benchmark results still pending, Mistral hopes ML4 will be best in class among open-weight models, especially outside of China, but not only, Stock said. Thanks to focused training, it could also outperform closed models in specific areas that are key to its customers, and where multimodal capabilities can add value.
According to Stock, ML4’s optimized use cases include cybersecurity and finance, but also chip design, which is core to two of Mistral’s main backers — Dutch giant ASML, which led its Series C, and Samsung, which led its Series D last month at a €21 billion valuation (about $24.39 billion).
At the time, the company tried to convey that its decision to host Chinese models wasn’t a pivot into becoming a mere inference provider. With Le Chonk in its corner, the company believes it should still be considered a frontier lab as well.

title_en: Controversial $110 billion mega-merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. finally closes
title_fa: Controversial $110 billion mega-merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. finally closes
excerpt_en: New media empire will be known as Skydance, with CEO David Ellision calling it a 'historic day.'
excerpt_fa: New media empire will be known as Skydance, with CEO David Ellision calling it a 'historic day.'
content_en:
Controversial $110 billion mega-merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. finally closes
New media empire will be known as Skydance, with CEO David Ellision calling it a ‘historic day.'
After nearly a year of negotiations, opposition and regulatory hurdles, the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger has finally reached its conclusion, with the $110-billion deal finally closing today.
The company now known as Skydance assumes full control of two of the largest film studios in the world, as well as networks like CBS, CNN, MTV and Comedy Central. The streaming services HBO Max and Paramount Plus also now fall under the same roof. In a press release, Skydance said that between Paramount and WBD it has committed to putting out 30 theatrical films per year, as well as more than 180 TV shows and series.
The scale of this new media empire is enormous. The combined Skydance portfolio includes DC, Harry Potter and the Game of Thrones IP, as well as the Mission: Impossible franchise, Lord of the Rings, Star Trek, Looney Tunes and SpongeBob SquarePants. TNT, Adult Swim, Cartoon Network and Nickelodeon all also now belong to the same company following completion of the merger.
Skydance will start trading on the New York Stock Exchange as SKYD today, as shares in WBD cease trading on NASDAQ. The company's total annual revenue is now nearly $70 billion, though as Variety reports, the mega-merger will immediately be saddled with $80 billion in debt.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Skydance CEO David Ellison in a statement. "From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality."
Last week Ellison announced that his new company would adopt the name Skydance, the same name he used for the first production company he formed in 2006. The Warner Bros. acquisition comes after Skydance closed its $8 billion deal to buy Paramount last summer, and successfully fought off competition from Netflix.

title_en: The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video in 2027
title_fa: The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video in 2027
excerpt_en: Amazon is reportedly paying up to $25 million a year for exclusive global rights to the ceremony.
excerpt_fa: Amazon is reportedly paying up to $25 million a year for exclusive global rights to the ceremony.
content_en:
The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video in 2027
Amazon is reportedly paying up to $25 million a year for exclusive global rights to the ceremony.
Amazon has secured the exclusive rights to stream the Emmy Awards starting in 2027. You won't need to be an Amazon Prime subscriber to watch, as Prime Video will stream the ceremony for free across more than 240 counties and territories. The six-year deal with the Television Academy brings to an end the traditional annual rotation between broadcast networks ABC, CBS, FOX and NBC.
Prime Video may offer other programming from the Television Academy, such as the Hall of Fame ceremony. The Hollywood Reporter notes that it's not yet clear where viewers will be able to watch the Creative Arts Emmys going forward. Deadline reports Amazon is paying between $20 million and $25 million per year for the right to stream the main ceremony.
While there's a degree of irony in the most prestigious TV award ceremony no longer being broadcast on networks, streaming companies have been muscling into the Emmys for years. For instance, this year's best drama and comedy series winners (The Pitt and Widow's Bay) are both streaming exclusives.
The Emmys will be the first of the major entertainment award ceremonies to be broadcast exclusively on a streaming service. It's beating the Academy Awards to the punch. It was announced late last year that YouTube will be the exclusive home of the Oscars starting in 2029.

title_en: Pinterest’s AI now turns beauty Pins into action plans
title_fa: Pinterest’s AI now turns beauty Pins into action plans
excerpt_en: Pinterest’s new AI-powered Beauty Guides translate hair and nail Pins into salon terminology, with estimated costs, appointment times, and maintenance needs.
excerpt_fa: Pinterest’s new AI-powered Beauty Guides translate hair and nail Pins into salon terminology, with estimated costs, appointment times, and maintenance needs.
content_en:
Pinterest on Tuesday showed off a new feature that will leverage AI to take action on your saved inspiration from beauty-related Pins, like hair and nail ideas, and turn them into actionable plans you can take with you to the salon.
“Beauty Guides,” which are powered by the company’s visual intelligence and generative AI technology, Pinterest Intelligence, will translate Pins into terms and phrases used by stylists and nail artists that everyday users may not know, like “balayage,” “root melt,” or “almond nails.”
The feature is a small but practical way to introduce AI into users’ everyday lives, as it slots into something that people are already doing: bringing a photo of their inspiration to the salon. That’s useful to a large extent, but having the right terminology at hand while you discuss what parts of the look you want to edit or change can be useful as well.
Plus, the guides offer the sort of information that can help users plan for their visit, like the time each part of the process may take and the cost. (Balayage goes into the hundreds of dollars, so that’s information you might like to have up front!)
The action guides will show up when you tap on the “Get the Guide” button within the app, and will then offer details about what, specifically, you should ask for to achieve the same look, the time it takes, price range, and maintenance requirements, like how often you’ll need to trim, tone, or touch up, for instance.
At launch, the feature will work across Pins related to hairstyle, color, nail shape, and finish.

title_en: This remote-controlled wagon is silly but so very useful
title_fa: This remote-controlled wagon is silly but so very useful
excerpt_en: Confession: When BougeRV told me about its remote-controlled wagon with animated lighting, I called it in for a laugh, expecting to eviscerate it in a review. It's ridiculous, to be sure. But the DuneRover also proved very capable, with enough torque to flatten hills even when...
excerpt_fa: Confession: When BougeRV told me about its remote-controlled wagon with animated lighting, I called it in for a laugh, expecting to eviscerate it in a review. It's ridiculous, to be sure. But the DuneRover also proved very capable, with enough torque to flatten hills even when...
content_en:
Confession: When BougeRV told me about its remote-controlled wagon with animated lighting, I called it in for a laugh, expecting to eviscerate it in a review. It’s ridiculous, to be sure. But the DuneRover also proved very capable, with enough torque to flatten hills even when carrying over 200 pounds of gear. It can also traverse soft sand that defeats conventional wagons.
This remote-controlled wagon is silly but so very useful
BougeRV’s DuneRover is so good on hills and sand that you’ll forgive the disco lights.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
As someone who regularly uses a variety of wagons to haul all sorts of gear, the DuneRover is an epiphany. But what BougeRV sent me was a Kickstarter prototype — and it shows.
Production units won’t ship until February 2027. So, what follows is less of a review and more a risk assessment for those considering backing the Kickstarter. That way, you can decide whether it makes sense to lock down early-bird pricing at $467, a claimed 48 percent discount off the eventual $899 list price. (Though I’ll wager it’ll always be sold for some kind of discount.)
Frankly, $500 isn’t outlandish for a wagon. Prices start at around $40 for a rickety model that will only last a few months, $300 for something durable from a reputable brand, and closer to $800 at the top end. And none of those wagons provides a motorized assist.
Let’s begin with the dumb stuff. The wagon has LED light bars on the back that are on by default and could come in handy at a campsite after dark. You can turn them off via the app, but you have to do it every time you restart the wagon. The default for a battery-powered device used primarily during the day should obviously be off.
Then there’s the remote control. I think I know what happened here. The product designers had a choice: route a cable through all the folding mechanisms that separate the motor from the handle or make it wireless. Wireless won, and then someone from marketing said, ‘Hey, I’ve got an idea!’
I mean, a remote-controlled wagon is so absurd that it’s kind of fun, and it brought a lot of joyful finger-pointing to onlookers during my testing. Maybe that’s enough?
The DuneRover is no joke for hauling gear. It’s fitted with two brushless geared motors, each producing up to 400W of output and up to 33Nm of torque. The wagon is activated by a trigger embedded in the handle that you press naturally when you pull the cart. Walk faster and the wagon will roll faster. Sometimes the wagon will lurch forward on that initial pull before settling into your walking rhythm. It’s not dangerous, it’s just unexpected. Release the trigger on the handle, and the wagon stops, even on an incline.
Pulling an oversized load weighing over 200 pounds up a 10 percent grade required a modicum of effort — but just a tenth of what it would have taken without the motor assist. Even on that steep incline, the wagon stops (with an inch or two of rollback) just as soon as I let go of the trigger. Repeated stopping and starting on slopes did, however, seem to confuse the DuneRover, occasionally causing the motors to become jerky as soon as I started walking again. A simple on/off resumed normal operation.
The motors also regulate speed when walking downhill with a heavy load. With the trigger held down, the controller did a good job monitoring changes in acceleration and countering the wagon’s speed to maintain my walking pace. When I stopped, so did the wagon, even on that 10 percent grade with a 200-plus pound load.
The motors aren’t powerful enough to haul that same load through soft sand, however. The oversized beach wheels performed much better in sand with loads weighing about half that, and should be excellent for families carrying a cooler, snacks, beach umbrella, toddler, and toys for a day at the beach.
I like that the DuneRover easily transformed depending on what I needed to haul. The sides can be unzipped and folded flat to convert the wagon into a cart for hauling oversized items or a senior dog. You can also unzip the sides but leave the straps connected to create more volume inside the wagon. I used this configuration a lot. Just know that you’ll want to bring a few bungee cords or cargo nets to keep everything securely in place.
My prototype suffered from intermittent rolling resistance with the motor off. The wagon would roll along fine for five or six feet, but then the wheels attached to the motors would brake, drag along the ground, and then release after a second or two. BougeRV assures me this isn’t something that would be exhibited by its production wagons. I ended up just leaving the motor on throughout my testing, even when I didn’t need it. The 82.14Wh battery was more than up to the challenge.
I used the DuneRover to move gear out of a beach house along the same route where I tested BougeRV’s original electric wagon. Six times I pulled the DuneRover along a path with 5 percent grade on one end and a 10 percent grade on the other. After six kilometers (3.73 miles) of soft sand, hard asphalt, wooden ramps, and gravel, the battery still showed a 74 percent charge. Not bad.
The removable battery features a bi-directional 100W USB-C port, making it a rather capable power bank. It can also charge from a 100W solar panel plugged into its XT-60 jack, thanks to a built-in MPPT solar controller. The battery in my prototype is not protected against rain, so I tested it in dry conditions, though BougeRV promises “full-vehicle IPX6-rated protection” in the production wagon.
The DuneRover is a beast at 59.5 pounds (27kg) with the battery and wheels installed. It’s also rather chunky when it folds. The quick-release front wheels can be removed if a flatter pack is required.
Overall, I’m impressed with the prototype DuneRover I tested — it’s capable, versatile, and proved to be an enormous help over the last few weeks of moving things between a holiday home, home, and adventure...

Then there’s the remote control. I think I know what happened here. The product designers had a choice: route a cable through all the folding mechanisms that separate the motor from the handle or make it wireless. Wireless won, and then someone from marketing said, ‘Hey, I’ve got an idea!’
I mean, a remote-controlled wagon is so absurd that it’s kind of fun, and it brought a lot of joyful finger-pointing to onlookers during my testing. Maybe that’s enough?
The DuneRover is no joke for hauling gear. It’s fitted with two brushless geared motors, each producing up to 400W of output and up to 33Nm of torque. The wagon is activated by a trigger embedded in the handle that you press naturally when you pull the cart. Walk faster and the wagon will roll faster. Sometimes the wagon will lurch forward on that initial pull before settling into your walking rhythm. It’s not dangerous, it’s just unexpected. Release the trigger on the handle, and the wagon stops, even on an incline.
Pulling an oversized load weighing over 200 pounds up a 10 percent grade required a modicum of effort — but just a tenth of what it would have taken without the motor assist. Even on that steep incline, the wagon stops (with an inch or two of rollback) just as soon as I let go of the trigger. Repeated stopping and starting on slopes did, however, seem to confuse the DuneRover, occasionally causing the motors to become jerky as soon as I started walking again. A simple on/off resumed normal operation.
The motors also regulate speed when walking downhill with a heavy load. With the trigger held down, the controller did a good job monitoring changes in acceleration and countering the wagon’s speed to maintain my walking pace. When I stopped, so did the wagon, even on that 10 percent grade with a 200-plus pound load.
The motors aren’t powerful enough to haul that same load through soft sand, however. The oversized beach wheels performed much better in sand with loads weighing about half that, and should be excellent for families carrying a cooler, snacks, beach umbrella, toddler, and toys for a day at the beach.
I like that the DuneRover easily transformed depending on what I needed to haul. The sides can be unzipped and folded flat to convert the wagon into a cart for hauling oversized items or a senior dog. You can also unzip the sides but leave the straps connected to create more volume inside the wagon. I used this configuration a lot. Just know that you’ll want to bring a few bungee cords or cargo nets to keep everything securely in place.
My prototype suffered from intermittent rolling resistance with the motor off. The wagon would roll along fine for five or six feet, but then the wheels attached to the motors would brake, drag along the ground, and then release after a second or two. BougeRV assures me this isn’t something that would be exhibited by its production wagons. I ended up just leaving the motor on throughout my testing, even when I didn’t need it. The 82.14Wh battery was more than up to the challenge.
I used the DuneRover to move gear out of a beach house along the same route where I tested BougeRV’s original electric wagon. Six times I pulled the DuneRover along a path with 5 percent grade on one end and a 10 percent grade on the other. After six kilometers (3.73 miles) of soft sand, hard asphalt, wooden ramps, and gravel, the battery still showed a 74 percent charge. Not bad.
The removable battery features a bi-directional 100W USB-C port, making it a rather capable power bank. It can also charge from a 100W solar panel plugged into its XT-60 jack, thanks to a built-in MPPT solar controller. The battery in my prototype is not protected against rain, so I tested it in dry conditions, though BougeRV promises “full-vehicle IPX6-rated protection” in the production wagon.
The DuneRover is a beast at 59.5 pounds (27kg) with the battery and wheels installed. It’s also rather chunky when it folds. The quick-release front wheels can be removed if a flatter pack is required.
Overall, I’m impressed with the prototype DuneRover I tested — it’s capable, versatile, and proved to be an enormous help over the last few weeks of moving things between a holiday home, home, and adventure...
